questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is '1526'. Write a question about this chapter that has exactly this answer, and add two details from the chapter about what happened that year.
questions.a: Sample question: 'In which year did the First Battle of Panipat put a final end to the Delhi Sultanate?' Details (any two): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi; Babur relied heavily on gunpowder, field artillery and matchlock guns; the victory laid the foundation of the Mughal Empire and Babur assumed control of the Delhi throne; Babur was a Turkic-Mongol ruler and a descendant of Timur.
s: A question whose only answer is 1526
First correct detail about that year
Second correct detail about that year

questions.q: Using the chapter's two timelines, analyse how the political map was reshaped in three phases: Phase 1, the 13th and 14th centuries; Phase 2, the 16th century; Phase 3, the late 17th and 18th centuries. For each phase give two dated entries and say which power rose or fell. Then state what the phases have in common.
questions.a: Phase 1 (any two): 1206 Delhi Sultanate established; 1326 Mewar re-established; 1336 Vijayanagara established; 1347 Bahmani Sultanate established; 1398 Timur attacks Delhi. Phase 2 (any two): 1526 First Battle of Panipat (Babur ends the Sultanate and founds the Mughal Empire); 1556 Second Battle of Panipat (Akbar's decisive victory); 1565 Talikota (Vijayanagara city destroyed); 1576 Haldighati (Maharana Pratap forced to retreat). Phase 3 (any two): 1671 Saraighat (Ahoms defeat the Mughals); 1699 Khalsa formed; 1754 Maratha control of Delhi begins; 1799 Sikh Empire established. Common thread: war, alliances and conquest redrew boundaries again and again, and the leading power changed from phase to phase.
s: Phase 1: two correct dated entries and the power(s) that rose
Phase 2: two correct dated entries and who rose or fell
Phase 3: two correct dated entries and who challenged the Mughals
Comparison: the leading power changed from phase to phase
Common thread: warfare, alliances and conquest kept redrawing boundaries

questions.q:
A class quiz asks: 'When was the Delhi Sultanate established?' Ritu answers 1192. Her friend answers 1206. Both dates appear in the chapter, but only one is the date of establishment on its timeline.
(a) What does the chapter say happened in 1192, and which timeline entry carries the date 1206?
(b) How many years separate the two dates?
(c) From the chapter's wording about 1192 and the Sultanate, which of the two dates came first, and why?
(d) The quiz wants the date the book uses for the 'establishment of the Delhi Sultanate'. Decide which answer the quiz should mark correct, and say what the other date really marks.
questions.a: (a) In 1192 King Prithviraj Chauhan, who ruled parts of northwestern India, was defeated; the Delhi Sultanate was formed after that defeat. 1206 is the timeline entry 'Establishment of the Delhi Sultanate'. (b) 1206 - 1192 = 14 years. (c) 1192 came first: the chapter says the Sultanate was formed after the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan. (d) 1206 should be marked correct, because the timeline names it as the establishment. 1192 marks the earlier defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan, after which the Sultanate was formed.
s: Part (a): defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan in 1192; the 1206 entry is the establishment
Part (b): 14 years
Part (c): 1192 first, as the Sultanate was formed after the defeat
Part (d): 1206 is the establishment date; 1192 marks the earlier defeat

questions.q: A museum label beside an illustrative 12th-century bronze from Tamil Nadu reads: 'From India's medieval period, a dark age before modern science.' Which correction fits the way this chapter uses the word 'medieval'?
questions.a: Here it is only a borrowed label for the 11th to 17th centuries

questions.q: A classmate complains that this chapter gives 'too few dates to be useful'. (i) Explain why the book deliberately keeps few dates. (ii) Say what its timelines and maps are meant to help you do. (iii) Pick two dates from the timeline that together show a change in who held power in one region, and explain the change.
questions.a: (i) The 'Tapestry of the Past' chapters keep only the dates that mark important reference points. (ii) Revisiting the timelines keeps those reference points in mind; revisiting the maps helps you visualise the geography crossed by armies, common people, traders, scholars and spiritual figures. (iii) Sample: 1336 (Vijayanagara established) and 1565 (Battle of Talikota, Vijayanagara city destroyed): a southern power rose and was then broken by the Deccan Sultanates. Other valid pairs: 1206 and 1526 (Delhi passes from the Sultanate to the Mughals); 1699 and 1799 (from the Khalsa to a Sikh Empire).
s: Few dates: only important reference points are kept
Timelines as reference points; maps to visualise routes of armies, traders, scholars and others
A valid pair of dates with the change in power it shows

questions.q: True or False: 'The invasions that began in the early 11th century were the first time warfare reshaped India's political map.' Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. The book says India had seen much warfare in earlier periods. What was unprecedented from the early 11th century was the spate of invasions by people from outside the Subcontinent, from beyond the Hindu Kush.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: warfare was not new; the unprecedented feature was the run of invasions from outside the Subcontinent

questions.q: A student says: 'The Delhi Sultanate was still in existence when Vijayanagara was established in 1336, and still in existence when Timur attacked Delhi in 1398.' (a) Using the chapter's two timelines, check both parts of her statement. (b) For how many more years did the Sultanate last after 1336?
questions.a: (a) Both parts are right: the Sultanate was established in 1206 and its end came with Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, so 1336 and 1398 both fall inside its life. (b) 1526 - 1336 = 190 years.
s: Part (a): both right, since the Sultanate ran from 1206 to the First Battle of Panipat in 1526
Part (b): 190 years

questions.q: Riya's textbook writes 'Tughlaq' while a library book writes 'Tughluq'. She lists them in her notes as two separate dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate. What explains the two spellings?

questions.q: Use three timeline entries: 1206 (Delhi Sultanate established), 1398 (Timur attacks Delhi) and 1526 (First Battle of Panipat). (a) For each, say who acted and whether the entry marks a state being founded, damaged or ended. (b) How many years separate 1398 and 1526? (c) Which of the three shows an invader who did not found a state in India, and what does the book say he did?
questions.a: (a) 1206: a dynasty of Turkic-Afghan origin founded the Delhi Sultanate (a state founded). 1398: Timur, a Turkic-Mongol conqueror from Central Asia, attacked Delhi, then a thriving city (a state damaged). 1526: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, which put a final end to the Sultanate and laid the foundation of the Mughal Empire (a state ended and another founded). (b) 1526 - 1398 = 128 years. (c) 1398, Timur: he launched a devastating attack on Delhi, large numbers were killed or enslaved, the city was left in ruins, and he soon withdrew from India with huge plunder, leaving chaos behind.
s: Entry 1206: Turkic-Afghan dynasty, a Sultanate founded
Entry 1398: Timur's attack, a state damaged
Entry 1526: Babur ends the Sultanate and begins the Mughal Empire
Part (b): 128 years
Part (c): Timur; ruins, killings or enslavement, withdrawal with plunder

Territorial ambition and the reputed riches of India's cities

Escaping the Mongols and spreading his religion

questions.q: Kabir writes in his notes: 'Many invaders of this period were Turkic or Afghan, and they came to India only to plunder its wealth.' Test both halves of his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: the book says many of the invaders were Central Asian, Turkic or Afghan. The second half is wrong: India's reputed riches were one draw, but the invaders also came for territorial ambitions and often to spread their own versions of their religion, by force of violence if necessary.
s: Verdict: partly right
First half confirmed: many invaders were Central Asian, Turkic or Afghan
Second half corrected: territorial ambition and spreading religion by force were motives too

questions.q: (a) Which of the two Battles of Panipat on the chapter's second timeline came first, and by how many years was it followed by the other? (b) Using the entries' wording, say what each battle settled.
questions.a: (a) The First Battle (1526), followed 30 years later by the Second (1556). (b) 1526: Babur's victory established the Mughal Empire. 1556: Akbar's decisive victory.

Part (b): 1526 established the Mughal Empire; 1556 was Akbar's decisive victory

questions.q: Aarav says: 'The defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan in 1192 is not on the chapter's timeline, so the chapter must treat it as unimportant.' Test his claim using what the chapter says about its dates and about 1192.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. The book says it keeps as few dates as possible, only those that mark important reference points, so a date's absence from the timeline does not make an event unimportant. The chapter itself says the Delhi Sultanate was formed after the defeat in 1192 of King Prithviraj Chauhan, and begins its account of the Sultanate there.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The timelines keep as few dates as possible, so absence proves nothing about importance
The chapter names 1192 as the event after which the Sultanate was formed

questions.q: Taking the 16th century as the years 1501 to 1600, which set contains only events from the chapter's second timeline that fall in the 16th century?

(a) Which two entries on the second timeline name an Indian kingdom or ruler as the Mughals' opponent in their own wording, and in which years? (b) From the timeline's own wording, which of the two was a retreat and which a victory for the Indian side?
questions.a: (a) 1576 Battle of Haldighati (Maharana Pratap) and 1671 Battle of Saraighat (the Ahoms). The 1556 entry names no opponent. (b) Haldighati: Maharana Pratap was forced to retreat. Saraighat: the Ahoms defeat the Mughals.

Part (b): retreat at Haldighati; Ahom victory at Saraighat

questions.q:
The chapter's first timeline lists: 1326 Re-establishment of the Mewar Kingdom; 1336 Establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire; 1347 Establishment of the Bahmani Sultanate; 1398 Timur attacks Delhi. A student reads the first three entries and writes: 'Three new powers appeared within a few years, so the Delhi Sultanate was gaining new regions in the 14th century.'
(a) How many years separate the first and the third of these entries?
(b) Who founded the Vijayanagara kingdom, and what had they been before?
(c) What does the chapter call the emergence of independent regional sultanates such as the Bahmani Sultanate?
(d) Decide whether the three entries support the student's reading, or the opposite reading that powers were rising beyond Delhi's control. Name the two entries that settle it.
questions.a: (a) 1347 - 1326 = 21 years. (b) Harihara and Bukka Raya, who had initially served as governors under Muhammad bin Tughlaq. (c) Rebellions against the Delhi Sultanate. (d) The opposite reading is supported. The Vijayanagara kingdom (1336) was founded by former governors of Muhammad bin Tughlaq who rejected Delhi's authority, and the Bahmani Sultanate (1347) was one of the independent regional sultanates the chapter calls rebellions; both are powers rising outside Delhi's control, not regions Delhi gained. (The 1398 entry adds that by the end of the century Delhi itself lay in ruins.)
s: Part (a): 21 years
Part (b): Harihara and Bukka Raya, earlier governors under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Part (c): rebellions against the Sultanate
Part (d): the opposite reading, settled by the 1336 and 1347 entries

questions.q: A guide at the Red Fort says that Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled the whole Subcontinent for most of the 14th century as its only emperor since the Mauryas. Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: His rule over most of the Subcontinent was a first since the Mauryas but short-lived
o: His rule over most of the Subcontinent was a first since the Mauryas but short-lived
He never held more than a few districts around Delhi and Daulatabad during his whole reign
Most of the Subcontinent stayed united under his heirs for a long time after he died
His capital shift to Daulatabad brought lasting control

questions.q: An inscription in the Quwwat-ul-Islam ('Might of Islam') mosque in Delhi's Qutub Minar complex states that materials from 27 destroyed Hindu and Jain temples were used to build it. (i) When was its construction begun and by whom was it completed? (ii) Why is an inscription on the building itself strong evidence? (iii) Which pattern of the Sultanate period described in the chapter does it support?
questions.a: (i) It was begun in Qutub-ud-din Aibak's time, in the early 13th century, and completed by later sultans. (ii) It is a record made by the builders themselves and fixed on the structure, so it is not a later or hostile account; some of the reused temple materials can still be seen. (iii) The destruction of temples and seats of learning during the Sultanate's campaigns, and attacks on sacred images out of plunder and iconoclasm.
s: Begun in Aibak's time (early 13th century), completed by later sultans
The builders' own record on the building, with reused materials still visible
Supports the chapter's account of temples destroyed in this period

(a) What does the phrase 'for the first time since' tell you about the centuries between the Mauryas and him? (b) Why does the chapter call this dominance 'significant' yet 'short-lived'?
questions.a: (a) That in all those centuries no single ruler had held most of the Subcontinent. (b) Significant, because most of the Subcontinent was under one ruler; short-lived, because his ambitious schemes were often poorly executed (the capital shift and token currency both failed).
s: Part (a): no ruler had held most of the Subcontinent in the centuries between
Part (b): significant for the extent; short-lived because his schemes were poorly executed

questions.q: Compare the effect on the Delhi Sultanate of Ala-ud-din Khilji's campaigns and of Timur's attack. Cover who each was, what each did, and whether each left the Sultanate stronger or weaker.
questions.a: Ala-ud-din Khilji was a sultan of Delhi. At the turn of the 14th century he campaigned over large areas of north and central India, sacking and plundering many cities, and he repelled several Mongol invasions at a time when the Mongol Empire covered most of Asia. His slave-general Malik Kafur pushed south, and the plundered wealth financed the Sultanate's huge army. The Sultanate came out larger and better defended. Timur was a Turkic-Mongol conqueror from Central Asia, an outsider. At the end of the 14th century he attacked Delhi, then a thriving city; in his memoirs he gave his aims as war with the infidels and plunder. Large numbers were killed or enslaved, Delhi was left in ruins, and he withdrew with huge plunder, leaving chaos. The Sultanate came out weaker: the Lodis who followed ruled a much shrunken territory. So one built the Sultanate up, the other broke it down.
s: Ala-ud-din: a Delhi sultan; campaigns in north and central India and repulse of the Mongols
Ala-ud-din: Kafur's southern push and plunder financing the army; Sultanate strengthened
Timur: an outside Turkic-Mongol conqueror; his stated aims
Timur: Delhi ruined, people killed or enslaved, chaos; Sultanate weakened and shrunk under the Lodis
Comparison: one expanded and defended the Sultanate, the other devastated it

questions.q: Show that Malik Kafur's southern campaigns could not have been paid for with Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token copper coins.
questions.a: Malik Kafur was the slave-general of Ala-ud-din Khilji, who campaigned at the turn of the 14th century. The chapter says Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled Delhi 'a few decades later'. The token currency was his scheme, so it did not yet exist when Kafur's campaigns were fought; in any case the chapter says the plundered wealth helped finance the Sultanate's military apparatus.
s: Kafur served Ala-ud-din Khilji at the turn of the 14th century
Muhammad bin Tughlaq, and his token coins, came a few decades later
So the coins did not yet exist; the plundered wealth helped finance the military

o: In practice it was a burden and humiliation that pushed people to convert
It was paid by peasants as part of the land revenue collected by the iqtadar

questions.a: The wealth plundered on the way paid for its military apparatus
o: The wealth plundered on the way paid for its military apparatus

questions.q: Ala-ud-din Khilji both attacked and defended. (a) Give one example of each from the chapter. (b) Why did his defence matter so much, given what the chapter says about the Mongol Empire at the time?
questions.a: (a) Attack: he conducted campaigns over large areas of north and central India, sacking and plundering many cities. Defence: he repelled several invasions by Mongol forces. (b) The Mongols were trying to add India to their empire, which then covered most of Asia, so repelling them kept India out of that vast empire.
s: Part (a): one campaign of plunder and one repulse of Mongol invasions
Part (b): the Mongol Empire covered most of Asia and sought to add India

questions.q: Ala-ud-din Khilji's coin bears the inscription 'Sikander Sani' ('the second Alexander'). (a) What did he call himself on it? (b) Give one reason, supported by what the chapter says he did, why he might have chosen the name.
questions.a: (a) 'The second Alexander'. (b) Any reason linked to his conquests, such as: he campaigned over large areas of north and central India, sacking and plundering many cities, and sent Malik Kafur to conquer kingdoms in the south, so he saw himself as a conqueror on the scale of Alexander. (The chapter only asks why; a reasoned answer is accepted.)
s: Part (a): 'the second Alexander'
Part (b): a reasoned link to his wide conquests

questions.q: Compare Ala-ud-din Khilji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq as rulers of the Delhi Sultanate. Cover (a) how each extended the Sultanate's reach, (b) one scheme or defence for which each is known, (c) what the chapter says of the lasting result of each.
questions.a: (a) Ala-ud-din Khilji campaigned over large areas of north and central India and sent Malik Kafur south, conquering several kingdoms; Muhammad bin Tughlaq expanded the territories further, so that for the first time since the Mauryan Empire most of the Subcontinent was under one ruler. (b) Ala-ud-din repelled several Mongol invasions; Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital to Daulatabad and introduced token currency. (c) Ala-ud-din's campaigns brought plunder that financed an enormous military apparatus; Muhammad bin Tughlaq's dominance proved short-lived, his schemes were often poorly executed, and the capital shift and token currency both failed.
s: Ala-ud-din: campaigns north and central, and Kafur's push south
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: most of the Subcontinent under one ruler
Ala-ud-din: repelling the Mongols; Tughlaq: capital shift and token currency
Lasting result for Ala-ud-din: plunder financed the army
Lasting result for Tughlaq: short-lived dominance, failed schemes

questions.q:
Delhi in 1398 was, in the chapter's words, a thriving city. Timur attacked it, and the chapter says he soon withdrew from India with huge plunder. Yet the dynasty that followed, the Lodis, ruled a Sultanate whose territory had shrunk considerably. A student asks: 'If Timur went home, why did the Sultanate not simply win its lands back?'
(a) What did Timur leave behind in Delhi and in the country?
(b) Which dynasty emerged afterwards, and where does the chapter say it stood among the five?
(c) What cause does the chapter give for the shrinking of the Sultanate's territory?
(d) Explain the puzzle: why did Timur's withdrawal not restore the Sultanate?
questions.a: (a) Delhi was left in ruins and chaos was left behind; large numbers had been killed or enslaved. (b) The Lodis, the last of the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate. (c) Increasing resistance from other states and kingdoms within India. (d) The loss of territory did not come only from Timur: it came from resistance by states and kingdoms within India (the Eastern Gangas, Hoysalas, regional sultanates and others), which did not go away when he left, while Delhi itself had been left in ruins and chaos.
s: Part (a): Delhi in ruins and chaos, many killed or enslaved
Part (b): the Lodis, the last dynasty
Part (c): increasing resistance from other states and kingdoms within India
Part (d): the shrinking had its own cause, resistance from within India, so Timur's exit could not undo it

questions.q: The Delhi Sultanate lasted from 1206 to 1526, and the chapter says a sultan's average reign was hardly more than nine years. Roughly how many sultans does that suggest ruled in all?
questions.a: About 36
o: About 36
About 29
Close to 45
Just 12

questions.q: The chapter says that perhaps Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved his capital to Daulatabad because he thought its 'more central location would offer better control of the empire'. (a) What reason is suggested for the move? (b) Why does the chapter write 'perhaps' instead of stating it as a fact?
questions.a: (a) That the more central location of Daulatabad (then called Devagiri) would give better control of the empire. (b) The chapter is offering a likely motive, not reporting one he recorded; 'perhaps' tells the reader that the reason is a guess about his intentions.
s: Part (a): a more central location, for better control
Part (b): the motive is a guess, not a recorded fact

questions.q:
Match each situation from the Sultanate period in Column A with the term in Column B.
Column A: 1. Copper coins declared to carry the value of silver or gold coins  2. Breaking sacred images because they are considered idolatrous  3. A tax charged on non-Muslim subjects  4. An enslaved man rising to command the Sultan's army in the south
Column B: a. iconoclasm  b. token currency  c. jizya  d. slave-general
Meera says: 'The Delhi Sultanate was a stable state: five dynasties gave it continuity for more than three centuries.' Do you agree? Give your verdict with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the Sultanate period was marked by political instability. Successions were often violent: almost two sultans out of three seized power by eliminating their predecessor, so the average reign was hardly more than nine years. Five successive dynasties replacing one another is itself a sign of upheaval, not continuity, and by the Lodis' time its territory had shrunk considerably. (The remark that five dynasties replacing each other shows upheaval is an inference; the marked evidence is the book's two-in-three and nine-year figures.)
s: Verdict: disagree
Evidence (marked): about two sultans in three seized power by eliminating their predecessor; average reign hardly more than nine years
Link to the chapter's own wording: the period was marked by political instability and the territory had shrunk by the Lodis' time

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The jizya was levied on non-Muslim subjects to grant them protection and exemption from military service.
Reason (R): In practice, depending on the ruler, the jizya was a discriminatory tax that was an economic burden and a public humiliation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: 'Muhammad bin Tughlaq had ambitious schemes, but they were often poorly executed.' Justify this statement using both of his schemes described in the chapter. For each scheme say what he did and what actually happened. Then say which of the two the chapter itself calls 'a progressive idea', and what that tells you about why that scheme failed.
questions.a: Capital shift: he moved the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (then Devagiri); perhaps he thought its central location would give better control. People were forced to travel over 1,000 km, the plan misfired, and a few years later the capital went back to Delhi; according to some sources both transfers caused great loss of life. Token currency: he declared cheap copper coins to be tokens worth as much as silver or gold coins; this created confusion in trade and encouraged counterfeiting, and the economy declined. The chapter calls the token currency 'a progressive idea' because most of our currency today is token. So its failure came from how it was carried out and the conditions of the time (confusion and counterfeiting), not from the idea itself; both schemes show good aims poorly executed.
s: Capital shift: what he did and the suggested aim
Capital shift: what happened (forced march, return to Delhi, loss of life)
Token currency: what he did and what happened (confusion, counterfeiting, decline)
Token currency is the one called 'a progressive idea'
Inference: the failure lay in execution and conditions, not in the idea itself

questions.q:
Two illustrative plans are put to a sultan who has an army to feed. Plan 1: raid a rich southern city, which brings Rs 90 crore of plunder once, but the raid disrupts that region's trade and farming, so the region's yearly tax falls from Rs 12 crore to Rs 4 crore. Plan 2: leave the region alone and collect Rs 12 crore a year. (All figures are illustrative.)

The comparison shows that plunder pays only in the short run: the region's yearly tax falls, which is the damage to trade and farming that the chapter describes, and it is the realm that bears that cost after the plunder is spent.

Part (c): the 12th year

Rivals: Bahmani and the Deccan Sultanates, the Gajapatis
Peak: Krishnadevaraya's military dominance over the Deccan
Peak: cultural renaissance (patronage, Amuktamalyada, temple grants)
End: Talikota 1565, sack of the city, fragmentation under the Nayakas

s: Part (a): 'royal policy'; a section of the Amuktamalyada on good governance
Part (b): it is the king's own account of his ideas

questions.q:
Paes described Vijayanagara as 'as large as Rome' and 'the best provided city in the world', with streets and markets full of laden oxen. A modern visitor to Hampi sees only the ruins, including the Virupaksha temple, and asks: 'Did Paes make it all up?'
(a) What two things did Paes compare or praise, in the lines quoted?
(b) What happened to the city in 1565, and over how long?
(c) What did the chapter say was destroyed or lost?
(d) Explain why Paes's account and the ruins do not contradict each other, and what a reader must not conclude from either one alone.
questions.a: (a) He compared its size to Rome and called it the best provided city in the world (with groves, water and laden oxen in the markets). (b) After the Battle of Talikota a coalition of the Deccan Sultanates sacked the city over several months. (c) Houses, shops, buildings, palaces and most of its temples were destroyed, and much of its civilian population was massacred. (d) They describe different conditions: Paes describes a living, well supplied city, the ruins show what the sack left. Neither alone gives the whole story: Paes cannot tell us how the city ended, and the ruins alone cannot tell us how large and busy it had been.
s: Part (a): the comparison with Rome; best provided city
Part (b): sacked over several months after Talikota in 1565
Part (c): houses, shops, palaces, most temples; much of the population massacred
Part (d): different conditions in time; neither source alone gives the whole story

questions.q:
Illustratively, Portuguese traders land 300 horses on the western coast in one season. The king's buyers offer Rs 2 lakh a horse, and a rival kingdom offers Rs 3 lakh a horse for any horses the king does not take. Option A: the king buys 240 horses at Rs 2 lakh each, and the traders sell the other 60 to the rival at Rs 3 lakh each. Option B: the king buys 240 at Rs 2 lakh each and matches the rival's price of Rs 3 lakh for the last 60. (All figures are illustrative.)
(a) What reason does the chapter give for the king's very good treatment of Portuguese traders?
(b) How much more does the king spend under Option B than under Option A, in rupees crore?
(c) Name two rivals named in the chapter who might have bought the 60 horses.
(d) Which option is consistent with the king's reason as the chapter gives it? Decide, and say what the extra spending buys.
questions.a: (a) The king did not want them to go and sell those precious horses to enemy kingdoms. (b) Under A the king pays 240 x 2 = 480 lakh; under B he pays 480 + 60 x 3 = 660 lakh; the difference is 180 lakh = Rs 1.8 crore. (c) Any two of Bijapur, Golconda and the Gajapati rulers of Odisha. (d) Matching the rival's price for the last 60 horses (paying Rs 3 lakh each, as in the second plan), because the chapter says the king treated the traders very well so that the precious horses would not be sold to enemy kingdoms; the extra Rs 1.8 crore buys the 60 horses, which would otherwise go to a rival.
s: Part (a): so that the precious horses would not be sold to enemy kingdoms
Part (b): Rs 1.8 crore more
Part (c): two of Bijapur, Golconda, the Gajapatis
Part (d): matching the rival's price for the last 60, in line with the king's stated reason; the extra spending keeps them from a rival

questions.q: Sameer says: 'After Krishnadevaraya's death Vijayanagara slowly faded away; it ended without any violent event.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No, he is wrong. Krishnadevaraya died of illness in 1529, but in 1565 a coalition of the Deccan Sultanates defeated the Vijayanagara forces under Ramaraya at the Battle of Talikota. The city was sacked over several months: houses, shops, palaces and most temples were destroyed and much of its civilian population massacred. Only after this violent break did the empire fragment into Nayaka-ruled regions and end in the mid-17th century.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Talikota, 1565: defeat by the Deccan Sultanates' coalition
Sack of the city over months, then fragmentation under the Nayakas

questions.q: A student reads Babur's memoir and says: 'Babur hated India, so he stayed only because he was forced to.' Which line from the chapter best shows that his view was mixed?

o: He called India of 'few charms' yet noted its gold, silver and artisans

questions.q: Show that Akbar cannot have faced Ibrahim Lodi in battle.
questions.a: Ibrahim Lodi was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, which put a final end to the Delhi Sultanate. Akbar was declared emperor at 13 in 1556, so he was born around 1556 - 13 = 1543, seventeen years after that battle. Akbar was Babur's grandson; he was not yet born when Ibrahim Lodi fell.
s: Ibrahim Lodi fell to Babur at Panipat in 1526
Akbar was 13 in 1556, so born about 1543
So Akbar was born after Ibrahim Lodi's defeat and could not have fought him

questions.q: A tourist at Agra says that Shah Jahan built both the Taj Mahal and Humayun's tomb. (a) Which of these two monuments does the chapter credit to Shah Jahan? (b) What does the chapter actually say about Humayun's tomb?
questions.a: (a) The Taj Mahal at Agra; he is best remembered as its builder. (b) It lists the building of Humayun's tomb in Delhi as part of the same peak period of art and architecture, along with the Red Forts of Delhi and Agra, but does not name Shah Jahan as its builder, so the tourist's claim goes beyond the chapter.
s: Part (a): the Taj Mahal
Part (b): Humayun's tomb is listed as part of the period's flowering; no builder named

questions.q: Akbar was 25 when Chittor fell, in about 1568 (he was declared emperor at 13 in 1556). His reign ended in 1605, and its final 15 years brought fresh campaigns. Those campaigns therefore began about ___ years after Chittor fell.
'Akbar's reign was a blend of brutality and tolerance.' Compare and analyse this statement: give two examples of each, and explain what the chapter says changed over his reign.
questions.a: Brutality: at Chittor he besieged the fort for more than five months and ordered the massacre of some 30,000 civilians, with survivors enslaved; his victory message boasted of destroying temples and 'the signs of infidelity'. He also had Himu beheaded after the Second Battle of Panipat. Tolerance: he abolished the jizya and promoted sulh-i-kul ('peace with all'); he held interfaith dialogues, appointed Hindu officials to high positions and set up a house of translation for Sanskrit texts. Change: early on he followed his predecessors' examples; as his empire grew he increasingly used political strategies to stabilise it, and Abul Fazl records him saying he had once persecuted men into his faith but grew ashamed as he grew in knowledge. Limits: non-Muslims still rarely exceeded one-third of his officials, and his last 15 years saw fresh campaigns.
s: Brutality: first example
Brutality: second example
Tolerance: first example
Tolerance: second example
Change over time: early ruthlessness, later political strategies and his stated change of view

questions.q: Trace how Mughal power was founded, nearly lost and regained between 1526 and 1556. Give five points, naming the person who acted at each. (The chapter's own order of events here is loose, so the order of Humayun's reconquest and Himu's rule is not marked.)
questions.a: 1. Babur, thrown out of Samarkand and a descendant of Timur, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal Empire. 2. After Babur's death in 1530 his son Humayun struggled to hold the empire together. 3. Sher Shah Suri, a powerful Afghan leader, took advantage of this and established the Sur Empire over large parts of north India, introducing many lasting reforms. 4. Humayun soon reconquered the lost ground, so the Sur Empire was short-lived. 5. Himu, a commander and wazir under one of the last Suri rulers, captured Delhi and ruled it briefly as Hemchandra Vikramaditya; Akbar, Babur's grandson, confronted him at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556, Himu was captured and beheaded, and Akbar reclaimed Delhi for the Mughals.
s: Babur's victory at Panipat, 1526
Humayun's struggle after 1530
Sher Shah Suri's Sur Empire and its lasting reforms
Humayun's reconquest (order relative to Himu not marked)
Himu's brief rule in Delhi and Akbar's victory at the Second Battle of Panipat, 1556

o: His middle years were relatively peaceful, with fresh campaigns in his last fifteen

questions.q: (a) Babur found India a 'country of few charms'. Name two things he nevertheless praised about Hindustan in the Baburnama. (b) Which of these does the chapter suggest most influenced his decision to stay in India?
questions.a: (a) Any two: it was a large country with masses of gold and silver; the air in the rainy season was remarkably fine; there were countless artisans and workmen of every sort. (b) India's wealth: the chapter says that perhaps for these reasons, especially India's wealth, he decided to stay and build his empire rather than return to Central Asia.
s: Part (a): two things he praised (gold and silver, rainy-season air, artisans)
Part (b): India's wealth

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the work in Column B.
Column A: 1. A memoir that lists birds and fruit trees and also boasts of 'towers of skulls'  2. The 'Book of War', made at a house of translation  3. A record of Akbar's administration, including the ranks of officers  4. A Persian version of an epic, illustrated with 176 miniature paintings
Column B: a. Ain-i-Akbari  b. Razmnama  c. the Persian Ramayana  d. Baburnama
(a) Who was Sher Shah Suri, and what did he establish? (b) The chapter calls his empire 'short-lived' yet says his reforms were 'lasting'. Explain how both can be true.
questions.a: (a) A powerful Afghan leader who, taking advantage of Humayun's struggles, established the Sur Empire over large parts of north India. (b) 'Short-lived' refers to the empire as a state: Humayun soon reconquered the lost ground. 'Lasting' refers to the reforms he introduced, which outlived his empire. A state can fall quickly while its changes remain.
s: Part (a): Afghan leader who set up the Sur Empire in north India
Part (b): the state soon fell to Humayun, but its reforms outlived it

questions.q: Ritika says: 'Akbar won over the Rajputs through tolerance and alliances rather than by force.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. As his empire grew he used marriage alliances, welcomed Rajput leaders into his court, abolished the jizya and promoted sulh-i-kul, and he did gain the support of many Rajput rulers. But force came first: at Chittor he besieged the fort for more than five months, ordered the massacre of some 30,000 civilians and enslaved the survivors. So tolerance and alliances came alongside, and after, the use of force.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: alliances, Rajputs at court, jizya abolished, support of many Rajput rulers
Wrong part: the force used at Chittor, so alliances did not replace force

questions.q:
A class compares two statements by Akbar. Source A is the victory message he sent at about 25, after taking Chittor, boasting of 'a number of forts and towns' where he had 'established Islam' and of destroying temples 'all over Hindustan'. Source B is recorded by his court historian Abul Fazl: 'Formerly I persecuted men into conformity with my faith and deemed it Islam. As I grew in knowledge, I was overwhelmed with shame. Not being a Muslim myself, it was unmeet to force others to become such. What constancy is to be expected from proselytes on compulsion?'
(a) What approach to conquest does Source A show?
(b) What reason does Source B give against forcing others to convert?
(c) Source B was recorded by Akbar's own court historian. What limit does that put on using it alone as proof of a change?
(d) Which two actions described in the chapter confirm that his policy did change, and which one fact shows the limit of that change?
questions.a: (a) Conquest with religious zeal: occupying forts and towns, establishing Islam and destroying temples, in the manner of many of his predecessors. (b) That forced converts cannot be expected to stay constant, and that it was inappropriate to force others to convert. (c) It comes from his own court, so it is not an independent witness; it should be checked against what he actually did. (d) Confirming actions, any two: abolishing the jizya; marriage alliances and welcoming Rajput and regional leaders to court; promoting sulh-i-kul; appointing Hindu officials to high positions. Limit: non-Muslims were kept a minority in the higher administration, rarely exceeding one-third of officials.
s: Part (a): conquest with religious zeal, as his predecessors
Part (b): forced converts cannot be constant; forcing conversion is inappropriate
Part (c): recorded by his own court historian, so not independent
Part (d): two confirming actions, and the one-third limit

questions.q: True or False: 'Because Shah Jahan had to fight several rebellions, art and architecture declined in his reign.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says Shah Jahan fought several rebellions but is best remembered as the builder of the Taj Mahal, and that his period formed the peak of an immense flowering of art and architecture, which also included Humayun's tomb and the Red Forts of Delhi and Agra.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the period was the peak of a flowering of art and architecture, with the Taj Mahal

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'Sher Shah Suri'. Write a question about this chapter that has exactly this answer, and add two details from the chapter about him.
questions.a: Sample question: 'Which Afghan leader took advantage of Humayun's struggles to establish the Sur Empire over large parts of north India?' First correct detail
Second correct detail

questions.q: Compare Babur and Akbar as rulers who held Delhi. Cover (a) where each came from or how he came to the throne, (b) how each won the throne or secured Delhi in battle, (c) what each did to stay and rule in India, and (d) how their methods of ruling differed, with one example for each.
questions.a: (a) Babur was a Turkic-Mongol ruler, a descendant of Timur, thrown out of Samarkand; Akbar, Babur's grandson, was declared emperor at 13 on his father Humayun's accidental death. (b) Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) using gunpowder, field artillery and matchlock guns; Akbar confronted Himu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556) and reclaimed Delhi. (c) Babur decided to stay for India's wealth and build his empire there; Akbar set out to bring the Subcontinent under Mughal control and reigned almost fifty years. (d) Babur was cultured yet ruthless, slaughtering populations and erecting 'towers of skulls'; Akbar blended brutality, as at Chittor, with tolerance, using marriage alliances, abolishing the jizya and promoting sulh-i-kul.
s: Part (a): Babur's origin; Akbar's accession at 13
Part (b): the two Battles of Panipat
Part (c): Babur stayed for India's wealth; Akbar's reign and aim
Part (d): Babur's ruthlessness with an example
Part (d): Akbar's mix of brutality and tolerance with an example

questions.q:
Akbar could not read, yet a museum in Jaipur displays an illustrative page from a Persian translation of the Ramayana made at his court, one of 176 miniature paintings in that manuscript. A visitor finds it strange that an illiterate emperor stood behind such a project. A guide adds that Akbar also abolished the jizya and promoted sulh-i-kul.
(a) What was Akbar's 'house of translation', and where was it?
(b) Name two other texts translated there, and the language they were translated into.
(c) Explain the apparent puzzle of an illiterate emperor driving this work.
(d) The visitor concludes: 'So non-Muslims had an equal share of power in Akbar's government.' Judge this conclusion using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A centre at Fatehpur Sikri where major Sanskrit texts were translated into Persian. (b) Any two of the Mahabharata (Razmnama, the 'Book of War'), the Bhagavad Gita and the Panchatantra; into Persian. (c) Despite being illiterate, Akbar became keen to explore Persian and Indian texts and showed great interest in classical Indian thought; he invited scholars to his court, so the work did not depend on his reading the texts himself. (d) The conclusion goes too far. Translation and tolerance did not mean equal power: non-Muslims were kept a minority in the higher administration, rarely more than one-third of officials and often much less, and even among Muslims those of foreign origin were favoured.
s: Part (a): Fatehpur Sikri, Sanskrit texts into Persian
Part (b): two of Mahabharata/Razmnama, Bhagavad Gita, Panchatantra, into Persian
Part (c): his interest in Indian thought and invited scholars, not his own reading
Part (d): rejected, since non-Muslims rarely exceeded one-third of officials

questions.q: True or False: 'Jahangir was the first Mughal ruler to try to expand the empire into the Deccan.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says Jahangir tried to expand the empire into the Deccan, but it also says that Akbar's last fifteen years involved fresh military campaigns in Kashmir, Sindh, the Deccan and Afghanistan, so Akbar had already campaigned in the Deccan.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: Akbar's final campaigns already included the Deccan

questions.q:
A Class 8 project compares reign lengths from the chapter: Delhi sultans averaged about 9 years; Mughal emperors up to Aurangzeb about 27 years; all Mughal rulers, up to the end of the empire in the 19th century, about 16 years. Aurangzeb himself ruled from 1658 for almost 49 years.
(a) By this measure, which group had the longest-lasting rulers, and what does the Sultanate figure reflect, according to the chapter?
(b) By how many years did Aurangzeb's reign exceed the 27-year average?
(c) What does the fall from 27 to 16 imply about the rulers who came after Aurangzeb, and what reason does the chapter give for the Mughals' rapid decline after him?
(d) A student writes: 'Since Mughal reigns were long, Mughal successions were peaceful.' Spot the error, using the events of 1657-58.
questions.a: (a) The Mughal emperors up to Aurangzeb; the short Sultanate average reflects violent successions, with almost two sultans in three eliminating their predecessor. (b) About 22 years: 49 - 27 = 22, taking the chapter's 'almost 49' as 49. (c) The later rulers must have had much shorter reigns on average, pulling the overall figure down; the chapter says the Deccan wars depleted the treasury and strained the administration, a key factor in the rapid decline after his death in 1707. (d) Long reigns do not mean peaceful successions: in 1657-58 Aurangzeb defeated and executed his brother Dara, removed his two other brothers and imprisoned his father to take the throne.
s: Part (a): Mughals up to Aurangzeb; short Sultanate reigns reflect violent successions
Part (b): about 22 years (49 - 27, with 'almost 49' taken as 49)
Part (c): later reigns much shorter; Deccan wars drained treasury and administration
Part (d): the 1657-58 war of succession shows long reigns can start violently

questions.q: Karan says: 'We should leave the atrocities of this period out of our study, because people today bear no responsibility for what individuals did hundreds of years ago.' Test his claim against the chapter's 'Think about it' note.
questions.a: Partly right. His premise matches the chapter: we, today, bear no responsibility for the actions of individuals hundreds of years ago, since it is about people in the past, not people of today. His conclusion does not follow: the chapter says we need to know the facts of the past, and the victims of these atrocities deserve our respect and remembrance.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: no responsibility today for what individuals did centuries ago
Wrong part: we still need the facts, and the victims deserve respect and remembrance

questions.q: Vikram says: 'Aurangzeb ruled for almost 49 years, so he must have governed a calm and stable empire.' Do you agree? Give your verdict with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Length of reign is not the same as stability. The chapter says Aurangzeb was constantly faced with significant rebellions, spent the last 25 years of his life fighting war after war in the Deccan, and that maintaining those armies depleted the treasury and put a great strain on the administration, a key factor in the rapid decline of Mughal power after his death in 1707.
s: Verdict: disagree; a long reign is not proof of stability
Evidence: constant significant rebellions and 25 years of Deccan wars
Evidence: treasury depleted and administration strained, leading to rapid decline after 1707

questions.q: In his last letters to two of his sons, Aurangzeb wrote: 'I have not done well for the country and the people, and of the future there is no hope.' (a) Name one fact from the chapter that agrees with his judgement of his own rule. (b) Name one fact from the chapter that a defender could set against it.
questions.a: (a) Any one supported fact, such as: he reimposed the jizya and a pilgrimage tax; his 1669 farman led to the demolition of temples and schools; he persecuted Muslims of other sects, Sufis and Zoroastrians; the Deccan wars strained the administration. (b) Any one supported fact, such as: under him the empire reached its greatest expansion; he was a skilled soldier who conquered parts of the South.
s: Part (a): one chapter fact that agrees with his judgement
Part (b): one chapter fact that stands against it

questions.q: (a) To whom was Aurangzeb's 1669 farman addressed, and what did it order? (b) Why is an order issued in his own name stronger evidence of his motives than a historian's view that he acted only for political reasons?
questions.a: (a) The governors of all provinces, ordered 'to demolish schools and temples of the infidels and put down their teachings and religious practices'. (b) It is his own edict, stating the religious aim directly, whereas the political-motive view is a later scholars' interpretation; the chapter says the farmans make his personal religious motive clear too.
s: Part (a): governors of all provinces; demolish 'infidel' schools and temples
Part (b): his own words state the aim directly, unlike a later interpretation

questions.a: False. The chapter says some of the sultans of the Delhi Sultanate had already imposed the jizya; Akbar abolished it, and Aurangzeb reimposed it (together with a pilgrimage tax on Hindus).
s: Verdict: False

His grandfather Jahangir, who had lost the throne to him

questions.q:
An illustrative model of Aurangzeb's finances: his treasury holds a reserve of 200 units; each year it takes in 100 units of revenue and spends 70 units on the Deccan armies and 40 units on the rest of the administration. The model is a simplification (all figures are illustrative), but the chapter says the Deccan wars depleted the treasury.
(a) For how many years did Aurangzeb spend the last part of his life at war in the Deccan, according to the chapter?
(b) What is the model's yearly deficit, and in which year does the reserve run out?
(c) By the end of those years, what total shortfall does the model show beyond the reserve?
(d) Would cutting the Deccan armies' cost by 10 units a year have avoided the shortfall? Decide, and say what the chapter says maintaining those armies did.
questions.a: (a) 25 years. (b) Spending is 70 + 40 = 110 against income 100, so the deficit is 10 units a year; the 200-unit reserve lasts 200 / 10 = 20 years and runs out at the end of year 20. (c) Over 25 years the deficit totals 250 units; after the 200-unit reserve, the shortfall is 50 units. (d) Yes: cutting 10 units a year makes spending 100 and removes the deficit entirely. The chapter says maintaining the large armies for those campaigns depleted the empire's treasury and put a great strain on the administration.
s: Part (a): 25 years
Part (b): deficit 10 units a year; reserve gone after 20 years
Part (c): shortfall 50 units

questions.q:
An illustrative newspaper report from Delhi reads: 'On Republic Day the Sikh Regiment once again saluted the Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, a famous shopping area, before the President, as it has each year since 1979.' A reader writes in to ask why an army regiment honours a building in a market street.
(a) What event does the gurudwara mark, and in which year did it happen?
(b) On whose orders did it happen, and what had the Guru refused to do?
(c) How many years after that event did the regiment begin its annual salute, according to the chapter?
(d) Answer the reader: what does the chapter's own description of the site tell us about why a market-street building receives a military salute?
questions.a: (a) It marks the site where Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was beheaded in 1675. (b) Aurangzeb's orders; the Guru had refused to convert to Islam, even under torture. (c) 1979 - 1675 = 304 years. (d) The chapter calls the gurudwara a powerful symbol of faith and sacrifice and says it is uniquely honoured by the Sikh Regiment; the salute honours what happened there, not the shopping street around it.
s: Part (a): Guru Tegh Bahadur beheaded, 1675
Part (b): Aurangzeb; he refused to convert even under torture
Part (c): 304 years
Part (d): a symbol of faith and sacrifice, honoured for the event, not the place's use

questions.q: Preet says: 'The Khalsa was founded purely to attack the Mughals; defence had no part in it.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. The chapter describes the Khalsa as a martial brotherhood committed to justice, equality and defence of the faith, founded by Guru Gobind Singh in response to Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom; it frequently clashed with the Mughal forces, at great cost of life, but defence of the faith is named among its commitments.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Commitments named: justice, equality and defence of the faith
Origin in response to Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom; clashes with the Mughals came as a result

questions.q: A student says: 'The Sikh Empire was set up by the Marathas, who held Delhi from 1754.' (a) According to the chapter, who unified the Sikh confederacies into an empire, and when? (b) What role does the chapter actually give the Marathas in the Sikh story?
questions.a: (a) Maharaja Ranjit Singh, at the turn of the 19th century (the timeline marks 1799 for the establishment of the Sikh Empire). (b) As the Mughal Empire declined, especially under the onslaughts of the Marathas, several Sikh confederacies emerged in Punjab; the Marathas weakened the Mughals, but they did not found the Sikh Empire.
s: Part (a): Maharaja Ranjit Singh, at the turn of the 19th century
Part (b): Maratha onslaughts helped weaken the Mughals, so confederacies emerged; they did not unify them

questions.q: The chapter asks why Guru Tegh Bahadur endured torture rather than convert. Using the chapter, (i) describe what he endured, (ii) explain what he was standing up for, and (iii) say what his sacrifice led to.
questions.a: (i) Arrested on Aurangzeb's orders and ordered to convert to Islam, he refused despite torture and despite seeing three of his disciples tortured to death; he was publicly beheaded in Chandni Chowk in 1675. (ii) He had decided to stand with the Kashmiri Pandits who sought his protection from religious persecution, so giving in would have abandoned them and accepted forced conversion. (iii) His son Guru Gobind Singh responded by founding the Khalsa; the site of his martyrdom, the Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib, remains a powerful symbol of faith and sacrifice, saluted each year by the Sikh Regiment.
s: What he endured: torture, disciples killed, public beheading
What he stood for: protection of the persecuted Kashmiri Pandits, refusal of forced conversion
What it led to: the Khalsa, and a lasting symbol of faith and sacrifice

questions.q:
Class 8C pins five cards on a timeline about the Sikhs: 1675 Guru Tegh Bahadur beheaded in Delhi; 1699 Khalsa formed by Guru Gobind Singh; 1707 death of Aurangzeb; 1754 beginning of Maratha control of Delhi; 1799 establishment of the Sikh Empire. A teacher wants to label two gaps on the board: one 'the quick response to persecution' and one 'the long consolidation'.
(a) How many years separate the first two cards, and what does the chapter say the second event was a response to?
(b) How many years separate the Khalsa card and the Sikh Empire card?
(c) What does the chapter say emerged in Punjab between those two cards, as Mughal power declined?
(d) Decide which gap should carry which label, and justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 1699 - 1675 = 24 years; the Khalsa was established in response to Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom. (b) 1799 - 1699 = 100 years. (c) Several Sikh confederacies, which Maharaja Ranjit Singh later unified. (d) The 24-year gap, from the martyrdom to the Khalsa, is 'the quick response to persecution': the Guru's son founded the Khalsa in response. The 100-year gap is 'the long consolidation': through it, as Mughal power declined (the cards for 1707 and 1754 fall inside it), confederacies emerged, until Ranjit Singh unified them into a centralised empire.
s: Part (a): 24 years; a response to Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom
Part (b): 100 years
Part (c): several Sikh confederacies emerged
Part (d): 24 years is the quick response; 100 years is the long consolidation, with reasons

questions.q:
A student finds two descriptions of India in the late 1600s. Source P, by a European traveller, praises India as a land of abundance, with markets full of goods. Source Q, by a modern historian, says many peasants of that time lost their land. The student thinks the two cannot both be right.

(b) In whose hands was the wealth largely concentrated?
(c) Why did many peasants lose their land in the late 1600s?
(d) Judge whether a traveller's account of abundance, on its own, is good evidence for how a peasant lived, and explain how P and Q fit together.
questions.a: (a) That India was still a land of abundance. (b) Rulers, courtiers, high officials and the merchant class. (c) After taxes and payments to intermediary parties they were often left with only a small share of their produce, and many lost their land and became bonded labourers. (d) It is not good evidence on its own: a visiting traveller saw markets, cities and courts where the wealth was concentrated, not the peasant's share after taxes. P describes the country's overall wealth and Q describes how it was shared, so both can be right at once.
s: Part (a): India was a land of abundance
Part (b): rulers, courtiers, high officials, merchants
Part (c): small share left after taxes and intermediaries, so land lost and bonded labour
Part (d): a traveller's view misses the peasant's share; both sources fit

questions.q: The chapter records clashes over sacred sites, yet says that 'by and large, people of different faiths and communities lived peacefully side by side'. (i) What caused the clashes? (ii) What does the chapter give as the basis of everyday peace? (iii) Explain why both statements can be true at once.
questions.a: (i) Clashes arose among common people, especially over sacred sites that had been desecrated or destroyed under the rulers' sanction. (ii) People were economically dependent on each other, and a fair degree of cultural interaction created a shared heritage. (iii) The clashes were particular incidents tied to rulers' actions at certain sites, while ordinary life in villages, markets and trade depended on cooperation; so conflict existed, but it was not the normal state of everyday relations.
s: Cause of clashes: sacred sites desecrated under rulers' sanction
Basis of peace: economic dependence and shared heritage
Both true: particular clashes versus everyday cooperation

questions.q: Pooja says: 'Since rulers changed so often, trade between kingdoms must have stopped; no merchant could do business across political borders.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No, she is wrong. The hundi system let merchants transfer funds across political boundaries without carrying currency, making them less vulnerable to plunder; it worked across trade networks without the ruling classes. Trader communities such as the Marwaris became adept at working across different political regimes, with parallel systems of credit and trust independent of official structures. Indian goods were also exported through coastal and riverside towns such as Calicut, Surat and Hooghly.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Hundis moved funds across borders without carrying currency
Marwari credit networks across regimes, and busy export trade

questions.q: Under Akbar the traditional structures of village self-governance continued 'more or less undisturbed', while ministers were assigned to each of the twelve subahs. (a) At which level of government did Akbar leave things largely as they were? (b) Give one reason, supported by the chapter's account of his administration, why a ruler might leave that level alone.
questions.a: (a) At the village level. (b) Any supported reason, such as: the subahs and their ministers, with checks and balances, already gave the centre control above the village, so village structures could carry on locally; or leaving them kept the administration simple and the village's own officials in place. (A reasoned answer is accepted; the chapter states only that they continued undisturbed.)
s: Part (a): the village level
Part (b): a reasoned point tied to the subah structure above the village

questions.q: True or False: 'Both the Ahoms' paik system and Akbar's mansabdari system let a ruler raise a large force without keeping a permanent centralised army.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Under the paik system every able-bodied man gave labour or military service in exchange for land rights, so the Ahom rulers kept a large standing force without a permanent army. Under the mansabdari system each mansabdar kept a set number of troops and animals for his rank, so an army could be assembled at short notice without a permanent centralised army.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: paik service for land, and mansabdars' fixed troops, both avoided a permanent army

questions.q: Compare the administration of the Delhi Sultanate with Akbar's. Cover (a) the ruler and his ministers, (b) how territory was run, (c) how officers were rewarded and troops raised, and (d) who bore the burden of revenue under the Sultanate and how Akbar's finance minister set it. End with one way Akbar's system aimed at greater control.
questions.a: (a) Sultanate: the sultan held absolute authority as political and military head, assisted by a council of ministers in charge of departments. Akbar: the Diwan (finance), Mir Bakhshi (military), Khan-i-Saman (public works, trade, industry, agriculture, royal household) and Sadr (justice, religious and educational matters). (b) Sultanate: territories assigned to iqtadars who collected taxes. Akbar: twelve subahs, each with such ministers, further subdivided, with checks and balances; village self-governance continued. (c) Sultanate: iqtadars kept expenses and sent the surplus to the treasury for the army; posts not hereditary. Akbar: mansabdars kept set numbers of troops and animals by rank, were paid with jagirs and inspected regularly. (d) Sultanate: taxes were levied on trade at every stage and the burden fell most heavily on the peasantry, with some accounts of cruelty in extracting revenue. Akbar: Todar Mal made detailed surveys of crop yields and prices, set a price for each crop and began a survey of land. Greater control: checks and balances between officials and regular inspections of mansabdars.
s: Part (a): sultan and council versus Akbar's four named ministries
Part (b): iqtas versus twelve subahs with ministers
Part (c): iqtadars versus mansabdars paid with jagirs
Part (d): burden on the peasantry versus Todar Mal's surveys
Greater control: checks and balances, inspections

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say about the peasantry and famines in this period? (b) On what did relief depend, and what does that show about a peasant's security?
questions.a: (a) The peasantry suffered several severe famines. (b) Relief depended on the particular ruler's benevolence, so a peasant had no fixed assurance of help; his security depended on who ruled.

Part (b): relief depended on the ruler's benevolence, so no fixed assurance

questions.q: Aman says: 'Under the iqta system an iqtadar's post was not hereditary, yet iqtadars stayed loyal to the sultan.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter says the iqtadars were nobles assigned territories to collect taxes which, minus expenses, were to go to the Sultan's treasury; the system created a network of local administrators loyal to the central authority, but their posts were not hereditary.
s: Verdict: the claim is right
Posts were not hereditary
The system created a network of administrators loyal to the central authority, collecting taxes for the treasury

Match each task in Column A with the official in Akbar's administration who would handle it (Column B).

The chapter ends by describing India as 'economically prosperous on the whole but often politically unstable'. Justify both halves of this description, and then explain who shared least in the prosperity.
questions.a: Prosperous: agriculture was the mainstay, and irrigation allowed multiple food and non-food crops; crafts (textiles, weapons, ornaments) and ship-building thrived; goods were exported through Calicut, Surat, Masulipatnam and Hooghly, and India imported much less than it exported; guilds, jatis, hundis and temple economies kept the Subcontinent among the wealthiest regions. Politically unstable: dynasties rose and fell; Sultanate successions were violent; invasions such as Timur's ruined Delhi; Vijayanagara was sacked after Talikota; the Mughals faced constant rebellions and long wars. Shared least: peasants, who paid about one-fifth (sometimes half) of their produce, suffered famines, and in the late 1600s were often left with a small share, many becoming bonded labourers; craftspeople and labourers also faced harsh conditions, while wealth gathered among rulers, courtiers, officials and merchants.
s: Prosperity: agriculture and irrigation
Prosperity: crafts, trade surplus, credit and temple economies
Instability: two examples of political upheaval
Who shared least: peasants (revenue burden, famines, bonded labour)
Who shared least: craftspeople and labourers, with wealth concentrated at the top

questions.q:
Todar Mal's method used surveys of crop yields and prices. Two illustrative villages are surveyed. Village A grows wheat on 40 bighas yielding 10 maunds per bigha at half a rupaya per maund, and cotton on 25 bighas yielding 6 maunds per bigha at 2 rupayas per maund. Village B's produce is worth 1,200 rupayas by the same method. An official proposes instead to charge every village a flat 150 rupayas whatever it grows. (All figures are illustrative.)
(a) Name two things Todar Mal surveyed, and say what he then fixed for each crop.
(b) Find the total value of Village A's produce in rupayas.
(c) What does the state collect from each village at the typical share the chapter gives, and in all from the two villages, under Todar Mal's method and under the flat charge?
(d) Decide which method the state should use, and say which village gains from the flat charge.
questions.a: (a) Any two of crop yields, prices and the land of the empire; on the basis of yields and prices he fixed a price for each crop. (b) Wheat: 40 x 10 = 400 maunds x 0.5 = 200 rupayas. Cotton: 25 x 6 = 150 maunds x 2 = 300 rupayas. Total = 500 rupayas. (c) One-fifth: Village A 500/5 = 100 and Village B 1,200/5 = 240, so 340 rupayas in all; the flat charge gives 150 + 150 = 300 rupayas. (d) Todar Mal's method: it raises 40 rupayas more (340 against 300) and takes the same one-fifth from both villages, while the flat charge takes 30% of Village A's produce and only 12.5% of Village B's, so Village B gains from the flat charge.
s: Part (a): any two of yields, prices, land; a price fixed for each crop
Part (b): 500 rupayas
Part (c): 100 and 240, total 340 against 300 for the flat charge
Part (d): Todar Mal's method; Village B gains from the flat charge

questions.q: Explain how merchants and traders could carry on business across changing political regimes in this period. Cover (a) the hundi, (b) the Marwari traders, (c) temples as a source of credit, (d) guilds and jatis, and (e) why these arrangements left merchants less vulnerable to plunder.
questions.a: (a) A hundi was a written instruction to make payment to an individual; it could be carried across political borders and let transactions happen without carrying currency. (b) Trader communities such as the Marwaris became adept at operating across different regimes, developing parallel systems of credit and trust that functioned independently of official structures. (c) Temples provided merchants with credit and funded internal as well as maritime trade. (d) Decentralised systems such as shrenis (guilds) and jatis (professionally defined communities), with systems for credit, supported the economy. (e) Funds moved without coin could not be plundered on the road, and these networks worked without the participation of the ruling classes, so a change of ruler did not cut them off.
s: The hundi: written payment instruction carried across borders without currency
Marwari traders' parallel systems of credit and trust
Temples as a source of credit and funding for trade
Guilds (shrenis) and jatis as decentralised systems
Why merchants were less vulnerable to plunder and to changes of ruler

questions.q: (a) Name two duties of the sultan that the chapter quotes from contemporary chronicles. (b) Which of those duties explains why the sultan needed iqtadars?

(b) Collecting fees and taxes: iqtadars were assigned territories to collect taxes, which were needed to maintain the army.
s: Part (a): two quoted duties
Part (b): collecting fees and taxes, which iqtadars did
